1. The Origin and Definition of MOOCs
45.4s–113.4s · Score 0.95/10
Hook: MOOCs were born by translating open content initiatives into open teaching experiences.
Why: explains an important benefit of MOOCs — This is a strong, foundational statement explaining the origin and definition of MOOCs, highlighting an alternative approach to conventional education, which hooks educators curious about the MOOC concept.
Caption: George Siemens explains how MOOCs started at the University of Manitoba as an experiment to open up teaching as MIT did for content, coining the term Massive Open Online Courses to emphasize scale, online delivery, and open participation with no prerequisites.

2. Practical Advice for Creating and Running a MOOC
300.1s–495.6s · Score 0.98/10
Hook: The best way to learn is simply to run a MOOC and try it yourself.
Why: find clear, practical advice — This clip contains dense, practical guidance, directly aimed at educators who want to create MOOCs, hitting the clipper's preferences for practical advice with a compelling, optimistic tone, and it stands alone clearly.
Caption: George Siemens gives actionable advice to aspiring MOOC creators: start with a topic you're passionate about, involve colleagues, focus on learner engagement and content creation, plan support carefully, and embrace course evolution rather than expecting all to be pre-planned.

3. The Primary Benefits of MOOCs for Teachers and Learners
507.4s–605.2s · Score 0.93/10
Hook: MOOCs are about rich learning experiences and long-lasting global connections.
Why: explains an important benefit of MOOCs — This clip clearly explains an important benefit of MOOCs from a practical and optimistic perspective, offering an emotional hook for educators interested in the impact of MOOCs beyond content delivery.
Caption: George emphasizes that the biggest benefit of MOOCs both for teachers and students is the deeper learning and ability to connect into digital networks, resulting in sustained collaborations and even peer-reviewed publications beyond the course.

4. MOOCs Should Reflect Global Educational Diversity
611.3s–652.3s · Score 0.91/10
Hook: Educators everywhere should create MOOCs to export their own cultural values and perspectives, not just import others'.
Why: makes a surprising prediction about online learning — This is a strong, somewhat surprising prediction and challenge to conventional educational globalization trends, making a compelling hook for educators on LinkedIn or YouTube Shorts interested in education equity and global perspectives.
Caption: George encourages MOOC creation outside North America and Europe, stressing the value of diversifying the open education movement by bringing in different global attitudes and content, challenging the dominance of elite university models.

5. Different Models of MOOCs and Openness
219.4s–298.5s · Score 0.88/10
Hook: Not all MOOCs embrace the Open Education Movement equally—content openness varies greatly.
Why: challenges conventional education — This clip challenges assumptions about MOOCs, providing a critical perspective on openness that can hook educators interested in the philosophy and practical implementation of open education.
Caption: George contrasts his open, resource-sharing MOOC model with elite university platforms like Coursera and edX that restrict content reuse, highlighting the importance of openness and learner-generated content in true open education.

fields.text: Hello, I'm Andrea Santos, and I'm here with George Simmons in Pretoria, South Africa.
Hello, George.
Hi, Andrea.
Thanks for agreeing and giving us this interview.
Could you please tell us a little bit about what you do to start with?
Sure.
Well, I'm George Simmons, as I guess you're aware, and I'm with Athabasca University.
I'm a faculty member in the Center for Distance Education, and I'm also involved in research
through the Technology Enhanced Knowledge Research Institute at the university as well.
Okay, excellent.
Thank you.
And, George, can you please tell us about the creation of the concept of MOOCs, Massive
Open Online Courses?
Sure.
Well, actually, it started, I was at the University of Manitoba at the time, and one of the things
that we were exploring at the university is, you know, what is the difference between
the teaching component of education versus the content component?
And by that time already, there were quite a few initiatives by numerous universities
to open up content, and this was in 2008, and so we were thinking, and I was working
with Stephen Downs, and it was like, well, what if we started teaching, you know, we
did for teaching what MIT did for content?
And so we decided with the courses on connectivism and connective knowledge, and so our goal
was to have others experience this notion of distributed social network learning, and
we had the course as part of a certificate program in emerging technologies, and we had
our full limit of students that were registered for credit students, but we decided, well,
let's take the entire course, the content, and teach everything online, and we had about
2,300 students that joined in, and that's where the term Massive Open Online Courses
was coined to sort of allude to or to emphasize that this is a huge course, it's done online,
there's no criteria or prerequisites for people to join.
Oh, fantastic.
So it's been four years now that you've been offering MOOCs?
Yes.
Okay, okay.
So how many MOOCs have you offered so far, any idea?
I would say it's probably been about a dozen, and they've been in different topic areas.
Right.
The connectivism course I've done about four times now.
I've also done courses on, you know, emerging technologies.
I've done several on learning analytics, because that's an area of growing interest.
I've been involved on openness in education, as well as education futures.
We did one on personal learning environments and networks, and I think that might be about it.
So altogether, it's been about a dozen different offerings of courses.
The largest number that we had was one we did last year, the Change MOOC,
which we actually ran over a period of about almost just under a year, I should say,
and we had 36, 37 weeks in total.
So we've taken different formats.
We've run some that have been very short, only about four to six weeks,
and we've run some that have been much longer ongoing.
So with each issue or each time we run one of these courses,
we try to look at what are different ways of experimenting.
You know, we've experimented with the duration of content.
We've experimented with a lot of guest speakers.
We've experimented with different kinds of content formats
versus different kinds of learner creation formats.
So we're always trying to play with a different model or take what we did previously
and try and fix some of the errors that we noticed arising.
Oh, fantastic.
And what would you say is the relationship between MOOC course
and Open Education Resources and Open Education?
Well, it depends how they're run.
I think in our cases, we try to use Open Education Resources exclusively for the courses.
We want people to be able to access all the readings and all the videos.
So what we've done is used, you know, we have a heavy emphasis with Open Education Resources
and the Open Education Movement.
But there have been more recently open online courses
that have been run by larger university systems,
in particular the system of Stanford with the Coursera Project,
and it's now got, you know, well over a dozen universities involved.
Then there's the Udacity Initiative, which is also an open online course as well.
And then there's the new one coming up with edX, which is Harvard and MIT.
I would say that the model that we've run is more closely affiliated
with the Open Education Resources because we emphasize openness,
we emphasize users creating their own content and sharing it freely with others.
But we have had other issues like Coursera
where they don't necessarily make the content freely available.
They don't necessarily allow it to be repurposed by others or remixed.
So I think there's less of a relationship with those new emerging,
the huge elite university courses than the less of an affinity
with the Open Education Movement with those systems.
Okay, I see.
And what would be the advice you would give for someone wanting to create and run a MOOC?
It's a great question.
I think probably the biggest thing to do is to just say just try it.
I mean, you know, yes, there's a lot of design work
and a lot of activity that needs to go into running it.
But the best way to learn what needs to be done is to run one.
And so I encourage, you know, take a step back and look at it.
What's a topic area that you're passionate about as an instructor?
Because you'll find that it takes quite a bit of time and effort
to run your first open online course.
So look at something that you're passionate about.
Then see if you can involve a few other colleagues.
You know, maybe you have people in different systems, different universities,
or even in different countries.
And see if you can bring them into helping you run the course.
Look at, think carefully about the relationship between content
versus the curriculum that you're using,
as well as guest speakers and other people that you want to bring in.
Namely, are there, let's say, keynote speakers that you can bring in
to run a session one week?
So look at how you can augment the experience by bringing other people in.
Another aspect I'd really emphasize is look at what you want students
to be able to do and create.
We've emphasized that a big part of the course are the skills
that students develop in teaching and in running the course.
So what I mean is we want them to engage with others in discussion.
We want them to create their own content.
We want them to share that content and to connect with others.
So our emphasis with open courses is getting students to be connected

fields.caption: George Siemens explains how MOOCs started at the University of Manitoba as an experiment to open up teaching as MIT did for content, coining the term Massive Open Online Courses to emphasize scale, online delivery, and open participation with no prerequisites.

fields.lyrics:
[Intro]
Whispers of the morning breeze,
Calling me back to the trees,
Home is where my heart will stay,
Guided by the light of day.

[Verse 1]
Years away, I wandered far,
Chasing dreams beneath the stars,
But here the roots run deep and wide,
In every shadow, hope will hide.

[Chorus]
From the soil, the strength will grow,
Patiently the rivers flow;
Every step, a story told,
Building dreams on ground of gold.

[Verse 2]
Hands worn by the dust and sun,
A family’s journey just begun;
Though storms may come and doubts may rise,
Faith ignites the calmest skies.

[Chorus]
From the soil, the strength will grow,
Patiently the rivers flow;
Every step, a story told,
Building dreams on ground of gold.

[Bridge]
We walk together, side by side,
With hearts entwined, no need to hide;
Community, our steady flame,
Carrying forward every name.

[Outro]
Night falls but stars will gleam,
Tomorrow’s light, a shared dream,
From these hands, from this land,
Hope reborn, we make our stand.
